mcqs.question: What distinguishes a structural hazard from a data hazard?
options: A structural hazard only happens between a load and a store, never other instruction pairs
A structural hazard can only occur if branch prediction is disabled
A structural hazard is caused by hardware resource scarcity, not by one instruction depending on another's result
A structural hazard requires the compiler to have made a scheduling mistake
mcqs.explanation: Structural hazards are purely about two instructions wanting the same physical hardware unit simultaneously — no data dependency required. Data hazards, by contrast, involve one instruction actually needing a value another hasn't produced yet. Neither branch prediction nor compiler mistakes are the cause.

mcqs.question: Why do most real CPUs use split L1 instruction and data caches instead of one unified L1 cache?
options: Split caches are always cheaper to manufacture
A unified cache can't hold both instructions and data due to encoding differences
Split caches are required by the ISA specification
Splitting them gives fetch and data access independent ports, eliminating a structural hazard that would otherwise occur nearly every cycle
mcqs.explanation: Because IF runs every single cycle and MEM (for loads/stores) runs frequently too, a shared memory port would create a structural hazard constantly. Splitting into separate I-cache and D-caches removes that contention entirely. It isn't about manufacturing cost, encoding limits, or an ISA mandate.

mcqs.question: When a structural hazard forces a one-cycle stall on instruction 4, what happens to the instructions behind it in the pipeline?
options: They are also delayed by one cycle, since none can advance into a stage the stalled instruction still occupies
They are unaffected because pipeline stages are independent
They are flushed and must be re-fetched
They skip ahead of instruction 4 to avoid the stall
mcqs.explanation: A stall inserts a bubble that holds the affected instruction in place for a cycle; every instruction behind it is blocked from advancing into the stage it occupies, so the delay propagates down the pipeline by exactly one cycle. Nothing gets flushed or reordered — a stall, unlike a misprediction flush, just adds a bubble.
